topics.title: Acute ischemic stroke: reperfusion overview
topics.summary: Disabling deficit within 4.5 h: give IVT as fast as possible — tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) (AHA 2026, COR 1); tenecteplase was noninferior in AcT, ATTEST-2, TRACE-2 and ORIGINAL. Do not thrombolyse mild non-disabling deficits: PRISMS showed no benefit (sICH 3.2 vs 0%) and ARAMIS found DAPT noninferior. LVO: give IVT if eligible and start EVT without waiting for a response; EVT is indicated within 24 h for anterior LVO, including selected large cores, and for basilar occlusion with NIHSS ≥10.

recommendations.text: In adult AIS patients with disabling deficits (regardless of NIHSS score) who are eligible for IVT, faster treatment is recommended as it improves functional outcomes.

In adult AIS patients presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well who are eligible for IVT, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) is recommended to improve functional outcomes.

In eligible adult AIS patients presenting with mild, non-disabling stroke deficits (e.g., isolated sensory syndrome) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well, IVT is not recommended as it has not shown superiority over dual antiplatelet treatment for improving functional outcomes.

In AIS patients eligible for both IVT and EVT, IVT is recommended to be administered as rapidly as possible without waiting to observe clinical response or delaying EVT initiation, to improve treatment times and clinical outcomes.

consider: Is the deficit disabling regardless of the NIHSS total? If not (e.g., isolated sensory symptoms), give DAPT instead of IVT.
Do not wait for coagulation results unless an abnormality is suspected, or for MRI to count microbleeds (AHA 2026).
Minor stroke with a visible occlusion: TEMPO-2 found no benefit from tenecteplase and more deaths (5 vs 1%).
Wake-up stroke, large core, basilar, MeVO and the late window have dedicated cards.
topics.caution: Use the ischemic protocol for contraindications and dosing; this overview is not an eligibility checklist.

topics.title: Code stroke activation and prehospital LVO scales
topics.summary: Activate the stroke team for any acute focal deficit — EVT can be offered up to 24 h from last known well. Check glucose, and do not wait for creatinine before CTA. EMS should use a validated scale, pre-notify, and go to the closest stroke-capable hospital (AHA 2026, COR 1). RACE (face 0–2, arm 0–2, leg 0–2, gaze 0–1, aphasia or agnosia 0–2): a score ≥5 had 85% sensitivity and 68% specificity for LVO (PPV 42%, NPV 94%). Bypassing a local stroke center for a thrombectomy center did not improve outcome in RACECAT (cOR 1.03): fewer received IVT (47.5 vs 60.4%) and more had EVT (48.8 vs 39.4%).

recommendations.text: For patients with suspected stroke transported by ambulance, use of a brief validated stroke assessment tool by prefacility personnel is recommended to improve early stroke identification, including detection of large vessel occlusion.

For patients with suspected acute stroke, EMS transport is recommended to the closest appropriate stroke-capable facility (ASRH, PSC, TSC, or CSC) to minimize time to treatment, rather than to a non-stroke-capable facility.

consider: Aim to image as fast as possible (for example within 25 minutes); do not delay CTA/CTP for a serum creatinine.
Children: suspect stroke with any sudden focal deficit, including a first seizure.
Mobile stroke units shorten onset-to-treatment and improve outcome where available (COR 1).
A seizure, hypoglycemia or apparent mimic can coexist with stroke; keep the stroke pathway open until a clinician has reassessed.
topics.caution: Prehospital scales triage; they neither exclude LVO nor decide treatment.

topics.title: Suspected stroke mimics and thrombolysis
topics.summary: Do not delay IVT for a disabling, otherwise eligible deficit to exclude every mimic: in 9 series (392 mimics among 8,942 IVT-treated patients), sICH was 0.5% and orolingual edema 0.3% in mimics, a lower sICH risk than in true stroke (RR 0.33). Check glucose first; if a disabling deficit persists after correcting hypo- or hyperglycemia, IVT is recommended (AHA 2026, COR 1). FABS ≥3 (no facial droop, no AF history, age <50, SBP <150, seizure history, isolated sensory symptoms) identified mimics with 90% sensitivity and 91% specificity after a negative CT.

recommendations.text: In suspected ischemic stroke patients with severe hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, if disabling stroke symptoms persist despite correction to normoglycemia, IVT administration is recommended to improve functional outcomes.

consider: Look for seizure onset, prior identical episodes, migraine aura, functional signs and toxic-metabolic causes.
If the diagnosis stays uncertain and the deficit is disabling, the low harm in mimics favors treatment within standard eligibility.
Obtain MRI DWI afterwards and record whether stroke was confirmed.
topics.caution: Mimic data are observational and mostly alteplase-era; they do not override contraindications or a structural lesion on imaging.

topics.title: Stroke chameleons: commonly missed presentations
topics.summary: About 2% of ischemic strokes were missed in the emergency department (47 of 2,200 in Lausanne). Missed patients were younger, had fewer vascular risk factors, less eye deviation and more cerebellar strokes, and were often very mild or very severe. They were labeled as another neurological illness (43%), a non-neurological illness (17%), unexplained decreased consciousness (21%) or a coexisting disease (19%), and had worse 12-month outcomes and higher mortality.
consider: Acute dizziness or imbalance: examine gait and eye movements; cerebellar strokes are over-represented among misses.
Unexplained decreased consciousness was a common label — image the brain and vessels, including the posterior circulation.
A coexisting illness masked about one in five misses: a persistent deficit still needs a stroke review.
topics.caution: These are single-center retrospective data; the absence of these features does not exclude stroke.

topics.title: Post-thrombolysis hemorrhage and angioedema
topics.summary: Any neurological worsening after IVT needs an emergent CT. If hemorrhage is suspected or seen, follow the post-lytic ICH protocol: stop a running thrombolytic, send urgent labs including fibrinogen, and correct the fibrinolytic coagulopathy early — the mainstay of treatment, though based on expert opinion (AHA 2017). Orolingual angioedema occurred in about 1% with tenecteplase or alteplase (ATTEST-2); assess the airway first. Teams must be ready to treat bleeding and angioedema (AHA 2026, COR 1).

recommendations.text: Healthcare professionals are recommended to be prepared to treat potential emergent adverse effects of IVT, including bleeding complications and angioedema (which may cause partial airway obstruction), to reduce poor clinical outcomes.

consider: Take cryoprecipitate, antifibrinolytic and angioedema drug doses from the protected protocol; this card adds no doses.
Angioedema: protect the airway early, hold ACE inhibitors and follow the angioedema protocol.
Involve neurosurgery and hematology early; manage BP, glucose and temperature as for ICH.
topics.caution: No randomized evidence supports a specific sICH reversal regimen.

topics.title: CT perfusion and collateral imaging for late-window selection
topics.summary: Perfusion maps estimate hypoperfused tissue (Tmax >6 s) and core (markedly reduced relative CBF; below about 31% of the contralateral side best matched DWI in the derivation study). DEFUSE 3 target mismatch at 6–16 h: core <70 mL, hypoperfused-to-core ratio ≥1.8 and mismatch volume ≥15 mL. DAWN used clinical–core mismatch instead: core <21 mL at age ≥80 with NIHSS ≥10; <31 mL under 80 with NIHSS ≥10; <51 mL under 80 with NIHSS ≥20. Within 4.5 h, do not delay IVT for perfusion imaging. Collateral flow on CTA alone selected patients who still benefited from EVT at 6–24 h in MR CLEAN-LATE (cOR 1.67; sICH 7 vs 2%).

recommendations.text: In adult AIS patients eligible for IVT within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, treatment is recommended to be initiated as quickly as possible while ensuring safe administration, avoiding potential delays from additional multimodal neuroimaging (CTA/MRA, CT/MR perfusion).

In patients with suspected AIS who awaken with symptoms or have unknown time of onset 4.5 to 24 hours from last known well, CTP or MR DWI-PWI selection with automated postprocessing software can be useful to determine eligibility for extended-window IVT.

consider: Check for artifact: a poor contrast bolus or leukoaraiosis can make non-infarcted white matter look like core.
EVT at 6–24 h can be selected on NCCT ASPECTS (AHA 2026, COR 1); perfusion is adjunctive when immediately available (2a).
Perfusion selection supports IVT at 4.5–24 h (2a); large-core trials also accepted CTP cores (e.g., SELECT2 ≥50 mL).
topics.caution: Software thresholds estimate tissue fate; they are not exact infarct volumes or stand-alone exclusions.

topics.title: TIA: evaluation and disposition
topics.summary: Treat TIA as a stroke warning: MRI with DWI ideally within 24 h (about 40% show infarction, which makes it a stroke), head-and-neck vessel imaging in the ED regardless of ABCD2, and ECG, telemetry and troponin for all. Admit presumed symptomatic >50% extracranial or intracranial stenosis. High-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) or minor stroke within 24 h: aspirin plus clopidogrel with a loading dose for 21 days, then one agent. Discharge only with the workup arranged and TIA-clinic review, preferably within 48 h.

recommendations.text: Multimodal brain MRI is the preferred method to evaluate for acute ischemic infarct and ideally should be obtained within 24 hours of symptom onset. In cases where MRI with DWI can be obtained without delay, NCCT can be safely avoided in a stable patient with completely resolved symptoms.
Vessel imaging in the emergency department is warranted regardless of ABCD2 score or likelihood of admission.
Presumed symptomatic (>50%) extracranial or intracranial stenosis warrants hospital admission.

consider: Does the story fit focal ischemia (abrupt, maximal at onset, usually <60 min) or a mimic (marching symptoms, positive visual phenomena, migraine, seizure)?
ABCD2 omits posterior-circulation signs and stenosis; dual or crescendo TIA is high risk and may warrant admission whatever the score.
Suspected cardioembolism: arrange prolonged rhythm monitoring (30 days) within 6 months.
topics.caution: A normal CT does not exclude infarction; persisting or recurrent deficits need acute stroke reassessment.

topics.title: Spontaneous ICH: first-hour targets
topics.summary: Run the care bundle in the first hours (INTERACT3: better 6-month mRS, cOR 0.86): SBP <140 started early and reached within 1 h; glucose 6.1–7.8 mmol/L (7.8–10.0 with diabetes); temperature ≤37.5 °C; INR <1.5 after warfarin. Do not drop SBP below 130 in mild-to-moderate ICH (AHA 2022, harm; ATACH-2 at 110–139 gave no benefit and more renal adverse events, 9.0 vs 4.0%). Reverse anticoagulation immediately (see the reversal card). Severity scores frame discussion but must not alone limit care; defer new DNAR orders until at least the second full day.

recommendations.text: Initiating acute BP treatment within 2 hours of ICH onset and reaching the target within 1 hour can be beneficial to reduce hemorrhage expansion risk and improve functional outcome.

For patients with mild to moderate spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP 150-220 mm Hg, acutely lowering SBP to a target of 140 mm Hg (maintaining 130-150 mm Hg range) is safe and may be reasonable for improving functional outcomes.
Acute lowering of SBP to <130 mm Hg is potentially harmful in patients with mild to moderate spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP >150 mm Hg.

For patients with spontaneous ICH who lack preexisting documented wishes to limit life-sustaining therapy, aggressive care with postponement of new DNAR orders or withdrawal of support until at least the second full day of inpatient stay is reasonable to decrease mortality and improve functional outcome.

consider: Repeat CT within 24 h, sooner if the GCS falls, for expansion, hydrocephalus or swelling; early CTA can flag expansion risk.
Vascular imaging (CTA ± venography) for lobar ICH <70 y, deep/posterior fossa ICH <45 y, or 45–70 y without hypertension (AHA 2022, COR 1).
Cerebellar ICH, hydrocephalus or a large hematoma: call neurosurgery now (see the ICH surgery card).
No prophylactic antiseizure drugs; continuous EEG for unexplained or fluctuating mental status.
topics.caution: Intensive targets are less certain for large or surgical hematomas; avoid SBP drops >70 mm Hg or below 110 (ESO 2026 consensus).

topics.title: ICH: when to revisit surgical options
topics.summary: Cerebellar ICH with deterioration, brainstem compression, hydrocephalus or volume ≥15 mL: immediate evacuation with or without EVD (AHA 2022, COR 1). Supratentorial ICH >20–30 mL with GCS 5–12: minimally invasive evacuation can reduce mortality (2a). ENRICH (lobar or anterior basal ganglia, 30–80 mL, within 24 h) improved 180-day utility-weighted mRS, mainly in lobar ICH; MIND (mostly deep, within 72 h) and SWITCH (decompression for severe deep ICH) were not conclusive. Large IVH with reduced consciousness: EVD (COR 1).

recommendations.text: For patients with cerebellar ICH who are deteriorating neurologically, have brainstem compression and/or hydrocephalus from ventricular obstruction, or have cerebellar ICH volume ≥15 mL, immediate surgical removal of the hemorrhage with or without EVD is recommended in preference to medical management alone to reduce mortality.

Minimally invasive hematoma evacuation (endoscopic or stereotactic aspiration, with or without thrombolytic use) can be useful to reduce mortality compared with medical management alone for patients with supratentorial ICH >20-30 mL and GCS 5-12.
EVD is recommended over medical management alone for patients with spontaneous ICH, large IVH, and impaired level of consciousness to reduce mortality.

consider: Location, volume, GCS, premorbid function and hours from onset decide which trial applies.
Craniotomy is a lifesaving option for deteriorating supratentorial ICH (2b); decompressive craniectomy may reduce mortality in comatose patients with large hematomas or refractory ICP (2b).
Agree on realistic goals with the family before surgery.
topics.caution: Lower mortality is not the same as better function; do not extend lobar-ICH results to deep or infratentorial bleeds.

topics.title: Aneurysmal SAH: coordinated specialist care
topics.summary: Secure the aneurysm as early as feasible, preferably within 24 h (AHA 2023, COR 1; ESO 2026 consensus), at a high-volume center. Start enteral nimodipine early (COR 1). Until it is secured: frequent BP checks with short-acting agents, avoiding hypotension, hypertension and swings; ESO suggests targeting about 160 if SBP stays >160–180 after analgesia and nimodipine. Good grade and equally suitable for both: coil rather than clip. No routine antifibrinolytics, statins, magnesium or prophylactic hypervolemia. EVD for acute symptomatic hydrocephalus.

recommendations.text: Surgical or endovascular treatment of the ruptured aneurysm is recommended as early as feasible after presentation, preferably within 24 hours of onset, to improve outcome.
Early initiation of enteral nimodipine is recommended in aSAH patients to prevent DCI and improve functional outcomes.

Frequent blood pressure monitoring and management with short-acting agents is recommended in aSAH patients with an unsecured aneurysm, targeting avoidance of severe hypotension, hypertension, and BP variability.
For good-grade aSAH from anterior circulation aneurysms equally suitable for primary coiling and clipping, primary coiling is recommended over clipping to improve 1-year functional outcome.

consider: New decline: think rebleeding, hydrocephalus, DCI/vasospasm or seizures — urgent CT ± CTA/CTP.
Seizure prophylaxis only with high-risk features (MCA aneurysm, high grade, ICH, hydrocephalus, cortical infarct); avoid phenytoin; stop by 7 days after an onset seizure.
Keep euvolemia; liberal transfusion (Hb ≤10 g/dL) did not improve 12-month outcome (SAHaRA).
topics.caution: Prophylactic hemodynamic augmentation and induced hypervolemia are harmful.

topics.title: Cerebral venous thrombosis
topics.summary: Anticoagulate on diagnosis, even with venous hemorrhage: parenteral heparin (LMWH favored), then oral anticoagulation for 3–12 months, or indefinitely with chronic major risk factors or recurrent VTE (AHA 2024). DOACs are a reasonable alternative to warfarin after the lead-in: RE-SPECT CVT (dabigatran) had no recurrent VTE and major bleeding 1.7 vs 3.3%; ACTION-CVT (observational) found similar recurrence and less major hemorrhage (aHR 0.35). Endovascular therapy is rescue only (TO-ACT: no benefit); decompressive craniectomy is lifesaving with impending herniation.

recommendations.text: The mainstream initial treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis includes parenteral heparin followed by transition to oral vitamin K antagonists for 3 to 12 months, depending on the underlying cause, or indefinitely in the presence of chronic major risk factors or recurrent venous thromboembolism.

The presence of venous hemorrhage does not constitute a contraindication for anticoagulation. Whether degree of venous recanalization should inform duration of anticoagulation remains an area of uncertainty.

Given the lack of controlled studies (and poorer outcomes in meta-analyses), endovascular therapies are reserved for patients with evidence of thrombus propagation, for individuals with neurological deterioration despite medical therapy, or for those with contraindications to anticoagulation.

consider: Confirm with MRI/MRV (CT/CTV is a reasonable alternative); add GRE/SWI or contrast MRV for cortical vein thrombosis.

Look for pregnancy/puerperium, estrogen, obesity, APS, myeloproliferative disease, malignancy and infection; headache with thrombocytopenia after an adenoviral vaccine suggests VITT — avoid heparin and involve hematology.
Watch vision, seizures and consciousness; escalate for deterioration or propagation despite anticoagulation.
topics.caution: Use LMWH in pregnancy; DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding and carry more thrombotic events in APS.

topics.title: Acute dizziness: HINTS and when to image
topics.summary: Sort dizziness by timing and triggers (GRACE-3). In acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo with nystagmus, nausea, head-motion intolerance, unsteady gait) and vascular risk, a trained examiner's HINTS beats early MRI: any central sign — normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation — was 100% sensitive and 96% specific for stroke; adding new hearing loss (HINTS plus) reached 99.2% sensitivity for central causes. Early DWI missed 12–14% of infarcts within 48 h. Central or equivocal findings: MRI/MRA. ABCD2 is not a dizziness screen (sensitivity 61%).
consider: Head impulse: a corrective saccade suggests a peripheral lesion; a normal head impulse in continuous vertigo is a central sign.
Nystagmus: direction-changing nystagmus on eccentric gaze is central.
Test of skew (cross-cover): any vertical misalignment is central and points to the brainstem.
Hearing: new hearing loss is the "plus" that raises sensitivity for central causes; triggered positional episodes are not a HINTS situation.
topics.caution: HINTS needs continuous vertigo with nystagmus and a trained examiner; routine CT is not the GRACE-3 way to exclude a central cause.

topics.title: Inpatient stroke: complication review
topics.summary: Stroke-unit care with protocols: bedside swallow screen before any oral intake; treat fever to normothermia and look for its source; treat glucose <60 mg/dL and keep persistent hyperglycemia at 140–180 mg/dL (not 80–130); oxygen only for hypoxia, to keep SpO2 >94%; intermittent pneumatic compression for immobile patients and no elastic stockings; no routine bladder catheters or prophylactic antibiotics; no high-dose very early mobilization within 24 h (AHA 2026).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients, a bedside swallow screening prior to any oral intake is recommended to identify patients at increased aspiration risk.
In AIS patients, it is reasonable to treat persistent hyperglycemia to achieve blood glucose levels of 140-180 mg/dL with close monitoring to prevent worse functional outcomes.
In inpatient AIS patients with hyperglycemia, IV insulin targeting blood glucose of 80-130 mg/dL is not recommended as it does not improve 3-month functional outcomes.
In AIS patients with hyperthermia, targeting normothermia (including nurse-initiated fever management protocols) is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.
In AIS patients with impaired mobility and no contraindications, intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) in addition to routine care is recommended over routine care alone to reduce DVT risk.

consider: After IVT: BP <180/105 for at least 24 h; antiplatelets in the first 24 h only when a strong indication outweighs the uncertain risk.
Screen nutrition within 48 h and depression with a structured tool; start enteral feeding within 7 days if the patient cannot swallow.
After EVT: neurological checks, access site, the BP plan and urgent imaging for any decline.
topics.caution: Intensive targets backfire here: SBP <140 after successful EVT is harmful, and IV insulin to 80–130 mg/dL adds hypoglycemia without benefit.

topics.title: Follow-up imaging by diagnosis
topics.summary: TIA or minor stroke: MRI DWI within 24 h and head-and-neck vessel imaging in the ED. ICH: repeat CT within 24 h (sooner with decline) for expansion; CTA ± venography for lobar ICH <70 y, deep or posterior fossa ICH <45 y, or 45–70 y without hypertension; DSA if CTA suggests a macrovascular cause or for primary IVH; MRI/MRA if CTA is negative; repeat DSA at 3–6 months may be reasonable after a negative first study. aSAH: CTA/CTP and TCD for vasospasm; after adequately occluded coiling, image again at ≥12 months (ESO). CVT: MRI/MRV (CT/CTV acceptable); whether recanalization should guide anticoagulation duration is uncertain.
consider: Any neurological decline: urgent CT first (hemorrhage, swelling, hydrocephalus), then CTA if reocclusion or vasospasm is possible.
Ischemic stroke: noninvasive intracranial and vertebrobasilar imaging (CTA or MRA) identifies atherosclerosis, dissection and moyamoya (AHA 2021, 2a).
Established FMD: at least one brain-to-pelvis CTA or MRA (consensus).
topics.caution: Schedules are examples; image sooner whenever the examination changes.

topics.title: Anticoagulants: label and interaction review
topics.summary: Before reversal, procedures or switching, confirm the exact drug, dose, indication, last intake and current renal function against the U.S. label. AF and VTE dosing differ. Apixaban's AF dose adjustment combines age, weight and serum creatinine; edoxaban carries an upper creatinine-clearance restriction for AF; warfarin needs INR monitoring. Check P-gp/CYP3A4 interactions and feeding-tube or swallowing constraints.
consider: Are the indication, current formulation, last dose, adherence and any planned procedure established?
Are current renal function, weight, age and hepatic status appropriate for the specific label?
Have P-gp/CYP interactions, other antithrombotics and nonprescription products been checked?
Do food, swallowing or feeding-tube requirements affect reliable administration?
topics.caution: Creatinine clearance alone does not select a dose; check the full label with a pharmacist and use the ICH protocol for urgent reversal.

topics.title: AF after ischemic stroke: anticoagulation timing
topics.summary: Start the DOAC early once AF-associated ischemic stroke is confirmed and hemorrhage excluded. CATALYST (5,441 patients from 4 trials): starting within 4 days vs day 5 or later reduced 30-day recurrent ischemic stroke, sICH or unclassified stroke (2.1 vs 3.0%; OR 0.70), with identical sICH (0.4%). ELAN schedule: within 48 h for minor or moderate and day 6–7 for major imaging-defined infarcts. OPTIMAS: within 4 days was noninferior to days 7–14 (3.3% each).

recommendations.text: In carefully selected (e.g., milder severity) AIS patients with atrial fibrillation, a strategy of early oral anticoagulation post-stroke is low risk and is reasonable compared with delayed anticoagulation, although the efficacy of early anticoagulation for preventing early recurrent stroke is not established.

In stroke or TIA patients with AF who do not have moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve, a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban) is recommended over warfarin to reduce recurrent stroke risk.

consider: Size the infarct on imaging (ELAN categories), not by NIHSS alone; brain imaging before starting may be considered (AHA 2021, 2b).
Hemorrhagic transformation: starting or continuing anticoagulation may be considered case by case (AHA 2026, 2b).
TIA with AF: anticoagulate immediately (AHA 2021, 2a); use a DOAC over warfarin unless there is a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
topics.caution: Trial schedules guide but do not set an individual start date for very large infarcts or significant hemorrhagic transformation.

topics.title: Stroke mechanism, ESUS and rhythm monitoring
topics.summary: Define the mechanism before choosing prevention, with testing started within 48 h: brain CT or MRI, ECG, and CBC, coagulation, glucose, HbA1c, creatinine and lipids (AHA 2021, COR 1), plus carotid and intracranial vessel imaging. Cryptogenic stroke: echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring are reasonable (2a) — CRYSTAL AF found AF in 12.4 vs 2.0% at 12 months with an implantable monitor. ESUS: antiplatelet, not empiric anticoagulation — NAVIGATE ESUS (rivaroxaban), RE-SPECT ESUS (dabigatran) and ARCADIA (apixaban for atrial cardiopathy) were neutral.

ESUS: TEE, cardiac CT or cardiac MRI might be reasonable to find cardioaortic sources (2b).

topics.title: TOAST classification and stroke mechanism
topics.summary: TOAST sorts ischemic stroke into five subtypes: large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel occlusion, other determined etiology and undetermined etiology, each labeled possible or probable by the clinician's certainty; interrater agreement was high. Assign the subtype after brain imaging, vessel imaging and cardiac evaluation, because the mechanism decides prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulant, revascularization, PFO closure).
consider: An incomplete workup leaves the mechanism undetermined; it does not establish ESUS.
DWI pattern helps: a single deep lacune suggests small-vessel disease, scattered emboli in several territories a cardiac source, and a watershed pattern large-artery disease (AHA TIA statement).
Lateral medullary infarction (n=130): vertebral artery disease in 67% and PICA disease in 10%; mechanisms were large-vessel 50%, dissection 15%, small-vessel 13% and cardioembolic 5%.
topics.caution: TOAST was built to classify trial participants; it does not replace an individual mechanism review.

topics.summary: PFO closure is reasonable for ages 18–60 with nonlacunar stroke of undetermined cause after a full evaluation and a PFO with high-risk features (AHA 2021, 2a); without high-risk features the benefit is uncertain (2b). Closure adds AF (CLOSE 4.6 vs 0.9%) and venous thromboembolism (RESPECT).

Use RoPE and PASCAL to judge whether the PFO is likely causal.
Discuss procedural risk, AF and the long-term antiplatelet plan with the closure team.

topics.title: Carotid stenosis: symptoms, severity and referral
topics.summary: Symptomatic 70–99% stenosis: endarterectomy if perioperative stroke or death risk is <6% (AHA 2021, COR 1); 50–69%: endarterectomy depending on patient factors (COR 1); <50%: no revascularization (COR 3). Operate within 2 weeks of a nondisabling event (2a); at age ≥70 or within the first week, endarterectomy is preferred over stenting (2a). Asymptomatic ≥70%: CREST-2 found fewer 4-year events with stenting plus intensive medical management (2.8 vs 6.0%) but no significant benefit from endarterectomy (3.7 vs 5.3%); ACST-2 found stenting and endarterectomy similar (5-year non-procedural stroke 5.3 vs 4.5%).

recommendations.text: CEA is recommended for patients with TIA or nondisabling ischemic stroke within the past 6 months and ipsilateral severe (70-99%) carotid stenosis to reduce future stroke risk, provided the estimated perioperative morbidity and mortality is below 6%.

When carotid revascularization is indicated for TIA or nondisabling stroke, it is reasonable to perform the procedure within 2 weeks of the index event rather than delaying surgery, to increase the likelihood of a stroke-free outcome.

consider: How was the stenosis measured (NASCET), and does the lesion explain the event?
Large or disabling infarct, hemorrhage or near-occlusion: individualize timing with vascular surgery.
Everyone gets intensive medical therapy: antiplatelet, statin and BP control (COR 1).
topics.caution: CREST-2 ran two separate trials, so it does not compare stenting directly with endarterectomy.

topics.title: Symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis
topics.summary: Severe (70–99%) symptomatic intracranial stenosis within 30 days: aspirin plus clopidogrel for up to 90 days (AHA 2021, 2a; AAN 2022), high-intensity statin with LDL <70 mg/dL, long-term SBP <140 and exercise (COR 1). BASIS (China) tested submaximal balloon angioplasty in selected patients; it does not establish routine intervention.
consider: Confirm the stenosis is symptomatic and in the right territory; 50–69% stenosis gets medical therapy (stenting is harmful).
Write the DAPT stop date and the single agent to continue.
Recurrent events despite therapy: recheck adherence and mechanism; the usefulness of angioplasty or stenting is unknown (2b).

topics.title: Cervical artery dissection
topics.summary: Give antithrombotic therapy for at least 3 months (AHA 2021, COR 1); aspirin or anticoagulation are both reasonable (AHA 2026, 2a). CADISS found no difference (stroke or death 3/126 vs 1/124); TREAT-CAD did not show aspirin noninferior to a vitamin K antagonist (composite 23 vs 15%; 7 ischemic strokes vs none). Reassess the regimen with symptoms and follow-up imaging.

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with extracranial carotid or vertebral arterial dissection, treatment with either antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for at least 3 months is reasonable to prevent recurrent stroke.

consider: Confirm on CTA or MRI/MRA and separate cervical from intracranial or aortic dissection.
Recurrent events despite antithrombotics: endovascular therapy may be considered (AHA 2021, 2b).
Look for an underlying arteriopathy such as FMD when the history suggests it.
topics.caution: Neither trial was powered to prove equivalence, and DOACs were not tested.

topics.title: Secondary prevention and medication review
topics.summary: Noncardioembolic stroke: antiplatelet rather than anticoagulant (COR 1); DAPT only short term (minor stroke/TIA 21–30 days; severe intracranial stenosis up to 90 days). BP <130/80 for most (AHA 2021, COR 1). Atherosclerotic stroke: statin ± ezetimibe to LDL <70 mg/dL (COR 1; Treat Stroke to Target events 8.5 vs 10.9%); no known coronary disease and LDL >100: atorvastatin 80 mg (SPARCL). Recheck lipids 4–12 weeks after a change, then every 3–12 months.

recommendations.text: Antiplatelet therapy is recommended over oral anticoagulation for patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA to reduce recurrent ischemic stroke and other cardiovascular events while minimizing bleeding risk.
An office BP goal of less than 130/80 mmHg is recommended for most hypertensive stroke or TIA patients to reduce recurrent stroke and vascular events.

For ischemic stroke or TIA patients with atherosclerotic disease (intracranial, carotid, aortic, or coronary), lipid-lowering therapy with a statin (plus ezetimibe if needed) to achieve an LDL-C goal below 70 mg/dL is recommended to reduce major cardiovascular events.

consider: Is the mechanism settled, and does it change the drug (AF, PFO, dissection, intracranial stenosis)?
Very high risk with LDL >70 despite statin plus ezetimibe: a PCSK9 inhibitor is reasonable (2a).
Check adherence, cost, smoking, diet and activity at every visit.
topics.caution: Avoid indefinite DAPT or antiplatelet-plus-anticoagulant combinations without a separate indication.

topics.title: Recovery, rehabilitation and follow-up
topics.summary: Start formal interdisciplinary rehabilitation assessment in hospital (AHA 2026, COR 1) and avoid high-dose mobilization within 24 h (COR 3: Harm). Reassess function, mood and goals at follow-up and re-engage therapy when needs change.
consider: Which impairments, daily activities and participation goals need assessment or renewed therapy?
Have the patient and care partner received education, training and support?
Is follow-up feasible (transport, access, telehealth), and who reassesses progress?
topics.caution: A screening score is not a diagnosis, and this card gives no driving, work or travel clearance.

topics.title: Pregnancy and postpartum stroke
topics.summary: Pregnancy should not delay stroke evaluation or treatment: image without delay (CT with or without contrast, and MRI without contrast, are considered safe), and IVT and EVT are supported when benefits outweigh risks (AHA 2026 maternal statement). Severe hypertension (≥160/110 confirmed within 15 minutes) is an emergency; magnesium and antihypertensives are the cornerstones for preeclampsia and eclampsia. Consider ICH, SAH, CVT, RCVS and PRES as well as ischemic stroke, especially postpartum.
consider: Establish the pregnancy or postpartum stage, blood pressure and likely mechanism.
Involve vascular neurology and maternal-fetal medicine early; a transradial approach is preferred for endovascular procedures when possible.
Plan for infant care, breastfeeding and rehabilitation support.
topics.caution: Acute stroke is not by itself an indication for delivery, and the statement supplies no universal antithrombotic choice.

topics.title: Stroke in neonates and children
topics.summary: Suspect stroke in any child with a sudden focal deficit, including a first seizure (AHA 2026, COR 1). Image with MRI/MRA, or CT/CTA if MRI is not available within 25 minutes (2a). Alteplase may be considered from 28 days to 18 years within 4.5 h for a disabling deficit (2b). EVT by experienced neurointerventionalists can be effective for LVO in children aged 6 or older within 24 h (2a) and may be reasonable from 28 days to 6 years (2b).

recommendations.text: In pediatric patients with sudden-onset focal neurological deficits, including first-time seizure, acute stroke is recommended to be suspected to enable timely diagnosis.

In pediatric patients aged 28 days to 18 years with confirmed AIS presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset with disabling deficits, IVT with alteplase may be considered as it appears safe, though efficacy is uncertain.

In pediatric patients 6 years or older with acute neurological symptoms from ischemic stroke due to LVO within 6 hours of symptom onset, EVT performed by experienced neurointerventionalists can be effective to improve functional outcomes.

consider: Call pediatric stroke expertise early and use age-appropriate imaging.
Consider age-specific mechanisms and mimics.
Follow-up should cover development, learning, family support and recurrence prevention.
topics.caution: Adult pathways cannot simply be transferred to neonates or children.

topics.title: Wake-up and extended-window thrombolysis
topics.summary: Unknown onset within 4.5 h of symptom recognition with DWI–FLAIR mismatch: IVT can be beneficial (AHA 2026, 2a; WAKE-UP: mRS 0–1 53.3 vs 41.8%). Perfusion mismatch at 4.5–9 h, or within 9 h of the sleep midpoint, without EVT: IVT is reasonable (2a; EXTEND: 35.4 vs 29.5%, sICH 6.2 vs 0.9%). LVO at 4.5–24 h with salvageable tissue and no EVT access: IVT may be beneficial (2b; TRACE-III tenecteplase 33.0 vs 24.2%, sICH 3.0 vs 0.8%). With EVT planned, late tenecteplase added nothing (TIMELESS; TNK-PLUS).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with unknown onset time who are within 4.5 hours of symptom recognition and have a DWI lesion smaller than one-third of MCA territory with no marked FLAIR signal change, IVT within 4.5 hours of symptom recognition can be beneficial to improve functional outcomes.

For AIS patients ineligible for EVT who have salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging, IVT can be beneficial within 4.5–9 hours of last known well or within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep for wake-up stroke.

In AIS patients with LVO and salvageable ischemic penumbra, presenting 4.5-24 hours from symptom onset or last known well, who cannot receive EVT, IVT directed by clinicians with expertise in thrombolytic stroke care may be beneficial to improve functional outcomes.

consider: Non-LVO at 4.5–24 h with perfusion mismatch (China): OPTION (tenecteplase; mRS 0–1 43.6 vs 34.2%, sICH 2.8 vs 0%) and HOPE (alteplase; 40 vs 26%, sICH 3.8 vs 0.5%) were positive.
Posterior circulation at 4.5–24 h, mostly mild, no EVT: EXPECTS (alteplase) functional independence 89.6 vs 72.6%.
Pin down last known well, symptom discovery and the imaging route (MRI mismatch vs automated perfusion).
topics.caution: Late-window benefit comes from imaging-selected, mostly Chinese cohorts and costs more sICH.

topics.title: Minor stroke, TIA and short-course antiplatelets
topics.summary: Noncardioembolic minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) within 24 h without IVT: aspirin plus clopidogrel with a loading dose for 21 days, then one agent (AHA 2026, COR 1). CHANCE: stroke 8.2 vs 11.7%; POINT: major ischemic events 5.0 vs 6.5% with major hemorrhage 0.9 vs 0.4%. Alternatives: ticagrelor plus aspirin for 30 days (NIHSS ≤5; THALES 5.5 vs 6.6%, severe bleeding 0.5 vs 0.1%); presumed atherosclerotic at 24–72 h: clopidogrel plus aspirin for 21 days (INSPIRES 7.3 vs 9.2%); CYP2C19 loss-of-function: ticagrelor plus aspirin (CHANCE-2 6.0 vs 7.6%).

recommendations.text: In patients with minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 3 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or greater) who did not receive IVT, DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel with loading dose) is recommended to be initiated within 24 hours of symptom onset and continued for 21 days, followed by single antiplatelet therapy, to reduce the 90-day risk of recurrent ischemic stroke.

In patients with recent (under 24 hours) minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 5 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 6 or greater, or symptomatic intracranial/extracranial stenosis 50% or greater) who did not receive IVT, DAPT with ticagrelor (including loading dose) plus aspirin for 30 days may be considered to reduce 30-day recurrent stroke risk.

In patients with minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 5 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or greater) within 24-72 hours of onset (or NIHSS 4-5 within 24 hours) who did not receive IVT and have presumed atherosclerotic cause (50% or greater intracranial or extracranial stenosis or acute infarctions of presumed large artery origin), DAPT (clopidogrel plus aspirin) for 21 days followed by SAPT is reasonable to reduce 90-day recurrent stroke risk.

consider: Disabling deficit? Assess for IVT/EVT first. Non-disabling: DAPT was noninferior to alteplase (ARAMIS), and alteplase gave no benefit (PRISMS).

topics.title: Thrombectomy selection and bridging thrombolysis
topics.summary: Anterior LVO (ICA or M1), NIHSS ≥6, prestroke mRS 0–1: EVT within 6 h if ASPECTS 3–10, and at 6–24 h if ASPECTS ≥6 (AHA 2026, COR 1). HERMES (≤6 h): mRS shift cOR 2.49; DAWN (6–24 h, clinical–core mismatch): mRS 0–2 49 vs 13%; DEFUSE 3 (6–16 h, perfusion mismatch): 45 vs 17%. Give IVT first when eligible and do not delay EVT: EVT alone was not shown noninferior in SWIFT DIRECT or MR CLEAN-NO IV, and BRIDGE-TNK favored tenecteplase first (mRS 0–2 52.9 vs 44.1%).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1), presenting within 6 hours of symptom onset, with NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, and ASPECTS 3-10, EVT (endovascular thrombectomy) is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting 6-24 hours from symptom onset, with NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, and ASPECTS 6 or greater, EVT is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, NIHSS 6 or greater, ASPECTS 6 or greater, and prestroke mRS of 2, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce accumulated disability.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, NIHSS 6 or greater, ASPECTS 6 or greater, and prestroke mRS of 3-4, EVT might be reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce accumulated disability.

consider: Prestroke mRS 2: EVT is reasonable (2a); mRS 3–4 within 6 h: EVT might be reasonable (2b).
Transfers: go straight to angiography without repeat imaging unless the exam changed or the transfer was delayed (2b).
Large core, basilar, MeVO and perfusion details: see the dedicated cards.
topics.caution: DIRECT-MT (China) found EVT alone noninferior, but European trials did not; give IVT whenever eligible.

topics.title: Large-core infarction and thrombectomy
topics.summary: Large cores still benefit: ASPECTS 3–5 at 6–24 h (age <80, mRS 0–1, no significant mass effect) is COR 1, and ASPECTS 0–2 within 6 h is reasonable (2a) (AHA 2026). recommendations.text: In selected patients with AIS from anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1), presenting 6-24 hours from symptom onset, age under 80, NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, ASPECTS 3-5, and without significant mass effect on imaging, EVT is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

consider: Measure the core consistently (NCCT/MRI ASPECTS or CTP core) and confirm age, baseline mRS and mass effect.

topics.title: Basilar artery occlusion
topics.summary: Basilar occlusion with NIHSS ≥10, PC-ASPECTS ≥6 and baseline mRS 0–1: EVT within 24 h (AHA 2026, COR 1). ATTENTION (≤12 h): mRS 0–3 46 vs 23%, mortality 37 vs 55%; BAOCHE (6–24 h): 46 vs 24%. NIHSS 6–9: benefit not established (2b; ESO suggests best medical treatment for NIHSS <10). Give IVT if eligible (ESO suggests IVT plus EVT over direct EVT); TRACE-5 tenecteplase within 24 h improved mRS 0–1 or return to baseline (38 vs 29%), but ATTENTION LATE found no gain from tenecteplase before EVT at 4.5–24 h (30 vs 30%).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with basilar artery occlusion, baseline mRS 0-1, NIHSS 10 or greater, and PC-ASPECTS 6 or greater (mild ischemic damage), EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset is recommended to achieve better functional outcome and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with basilar artery occlusion, baseline mRS 0-1, NIHSS 6-9, and PC-ASPECTS 6 or greater, the effectiveness of EVT within 24 hours for improving functional outcomes and reducing mortality is not well established.

consider: A low NIHSS can understate posterior-circulation disability; recheck for fluctuation.
Very extensive bilateral or brainstem infarction: ESO consensus suggests no reperfusion; with PC-ASPECTS 0–6, weigh age, frailty and prestroke disability.

topics.title: Medium and distal vessel occlusion
topics.summary: Routine EVT for medium or distal occlusion is not supported: DISTAL (n=543), ESCAPE-MeVO (n=530) and DISCOUNT (n=244, stopped for futility and excess sICH) showed no functional benefit, with more sICH (DISCOUNT 11 vs 3% among those treated) and higher mortality in ESCAPE-MeVO (13.3 vs 8.4%). ORIENTAL-MeVO (China, NIHSS ≥6, ≤24 h) is the only positive trial (mRS 0–2 58.6 vs 46.6%; sICH 4.7 vs 2.2%). EVT remains reasonable for a disabling dominant or proximal M2 occlusion (AHA 2026, 2a; SVIN 2026, 2a).

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with occlusion of the dominant proximal M2 division of the MCA presenting within 6 hours, prestroke mRS 0-1, NIHSS 6 or greater, and ASPECTS 6 or greater, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes, though benefits are uncertain.

In AIS patients with occlusion of the proximal nondominant or codominant M2 segment, distal MCA, anterior cerebral artery, or posterior cerebral artery, EVT is not recommended as it does not improve functional outcomes.

EVT is reasonable for patients with disabling stroke due to proximal and/or dominant M2 occlusions, particularly when associated with moderate-to-severe deficits and imaging evidence of salvageable brain tissue.

consider: Confirm the segment (dominant vs codominant/nondominant M2, M3, ACA, PCA), a disabling deficit and IVT eligibility; give IVT if eligible.
SVIN 2026: EVT may be considered case by case for disabling ACA or PCA occlusion; it is not standard for M3/M4.
Review ORIENTAL-MeVO's population limits with the intervention team.
topics.caution: The AHA 2026 grading predates ORIENTAL-MeVO and DISCOUNT; one positive Chinese trial does not establish benefit for every M2 or distal lesion.

topics.summary: Aim for eTICI 2b–3 as early as possible with a stent retriever, aspiration or both (AHA 2026, COR 1); general anesthesia or procedural sedation are both acceptable (COR 1). topics.title: Malignant infarction: hemicraniectomy and cerebellar decompression
topics.summary: Age ≤60 with unilateral MCA infarction deteriorating within 48 h despite medical therapy: decompressive craniectomy (AHA 2026, COR 1) — pooled DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET: survival 78 vs 29% and mRS ≤3 43 vs 21% (NNT 2 and 4). Over 60: may be considered to reduce mortality (2b); DESTINY II (61–82 y) doubled survival with mRS 0–4 (38 vs 18%), but no one reached mRS 0–2. Cerebellar infarction: ventriculostomy for obstructive hydrocephalus; suboccipital decompression for brainstem compression or volume ≥35 mL (COR 1).

recommendations.text: In patients 60 years of age or younger with unilateral MCA infarctions who deteriorate neurologically within 48 hours from brain swelling despite medical therapy, decompressive craniectomy with dural expansion is recommended to reduce mortality and improve functional outcome.

In patients over 60 years of age with unilateral MCA infarctions who deteriorate neurologically within 48 hours from brain swelling despite medical therapy, decompressive craniectomy with dural expansion may be considered to reduce mortality.

In patients with cerebellar infarction and obstructive hydrocephalus, ventriculostomy is recommended to improve neurological function and decrease mortality. Concomitant or subsequent decompressive craniectomy may or may not be necessary based on infarction size, neurological condition, degree of brainstem compression, and effectiveness of medical management.

In patients with cerebellar infarction causing neurological deterioration from brainstem compression or infarct volumes 35 mL or greater, decompressive suboccipital craniectomy with dural expansion is recommended to improve outcomes and decrease mortality.

consider: Discuss goals early and transfer large MCA or cerebellar infarcts to a neurosurgical center before they swell.
Falling consciousness from swelling is a reasonable trigger for surgery (2a); use osmotherapy only as a bridge.
Avoid hypothermia, barbiturates and corticosteroids for swelling; IV glibenclamide did not help (COR 3).
topics.caution: Surgery saves lives, but most older survivors need help with daily care; decide with the outcomes the patient would accept.

topics.title: Acute blood pressure targets by pathway
topics.summary: Before IVT <185/110; after IVT <180/105 for at least 24 h; during and for 24 h after EVT ≤180/105 (AHA 2026; ESO 2026). After successful EVT do not target SBP <140 (AHA 2026, harm): ENCHANTED2/MT (<120) worsened mRS (OR 1.37) and OPTIMAL-BP (<140) lowered mRS 0–2 from 54.4 to 39.4%. One Spanish trial (HOPE) found reperfusion-guided targets (140–160 for mTICI 2b; 100–140 for 2c/3) improved mRS 0–2 (60.0 vs 47.1%). No reperfusion and <220/120: starting treatment in the first 48–72 h does not help; ≥220/120: benefit uncertain (ESO: lower by <15% over 24 h). No routine prehospital lowering (INTERACT4: ischemic stroke cOR 1.30).

recommendations.text: AIS patients with elevated BP who are otherwise eligible for IVT are recommended to have SBP lowered below 185 mmHg and DBP below 110 mmHg before initiating IVT therapy to reduce hemorrhagic complications.
After IVT treatment, BP is recommended to be maintained below 180/105 mmHg for at least the first 24 hours.
In patients who undergo EVT, it is reasonable to maintain BP at or below 180/105 mmHg during and for 24 hours after the procedure.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation LVO who have been successfully recanalized by EVT (mTICI 2b, 2c, or 3) without other indications for specific BP targets, intensive SBP reduction to below 140 mmHg for the first 72 hours is harmful and not recommended.

In patients with mild to moderate severity AIS treated with IVT, intensive SBP reduction (target below 140 mmHg compared with below 180 mmHg) is not recommended as it does not improve functional outcome.

consider: After alteplase, SBP 130–140 did not improve outcome versus <180 (ENCHANTED; AHA 2026 COR 3).
Treat hypertension early only when a comorbidity demands it (ACS, heart failure, aortic dissection, post-IVT sICH, preeclampsia); correct hypotension and hypovolemia.
Hold home oral antihypertensives while swallowing is unsafe; ESO advises against routinely continuing them in the acute phase.
topics.caution: One number does not fit every pathway; ICH and long-term targets are on their own cards.

topics.title: Antithrombotic-associated ICH: reversal
topics.summary: Stop the drug and reverse as soon as ICH is diagnosed (AHA 2022, COR 1). Factor Xa inhibitor: 4F-PCC rather than andexanet (NCS/SCCM 2026, conditional); andexanet (Andexxa) was withdrawn from the US market effective 22 December 2025. Warfarin with INR ≥2.0: 4F-PCC over FFP, then IV vitamin K (COR 1). Dabigatran: idarucizumab (2a). Heparin: protamine (2a). Antiplatelets: no platelet transfusion unless neurosurgery is planned; if on aspirin and going to surgery, transfuse platelets (conditional). No recommendation on desmopressin or on reversal in small ICH.

recommendations.text: Immediate discontinuation of anticoagulation and rapid reversal are recommended as soon as possible after diagnosis of anticoagulant-associated spontaneous ICH to improve survival.
We suggest using 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate rather than andexanet alfa in patients with factor Xa inhibitor-associated spontaneous ICH.
We suggest against administering platelet transfusions to patients with spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage taking antiplatelet agents who do not require neurosurgical intervention.
We suggest administering platelet transfusions to patients with spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage who were on aspirin therapy who require neurosurgical intervention.
4-factor PCC is recommended over FFP for patients with VKA-associated spontaneous ICH and INR ≥ 2.0 to achieve rapid INR correction and limit hemorrhage expansion.
Idarucizumab is reasonable for patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH to reverse the anticoagulant effect.

consider: Record drug, dose, last intake and renal function; activated charcoal may help if a DOAC was taken within the previous few hours (2b).
Dabigatran without idarucizumab: PCC/aPCC or renal replacement therapy may be considered (2b).
Traumatic ICH: viscoelastic-assay-guided treatment if available (NCS/SCCM 2026).
topics.caution: ANNEXA-I's better hemostasis came with more thrombotic events and no functional gain; take doses from the ICH protocol.

topics.title: CAA, lobar hemorrhage and recurrence risk
topics.summary: Suspect CAA with lobar ICH, convexity SAH or transient focal episodes; MRI with blood-sensitive sequences looks for lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis. consider: Transient focal episodes may be CAA rather than TIA — avoid reflex antithrombotics.
Long-term BP <130/80 is reasonable after ICH (AHA 2022, 2a).
Ask about antiamyloid therapy; CAA changes those decisions.

topics.title: Seizures after stroke: treatment versus prophylaxis
topics.summary: Treat clinical or EEG-confirmed seizures. Do not give prophylactic antiseizure drugs after ischemic stroke or ICH without seizures (AHA 2026; AHA 2022: no benefit). recommendations.text: In adult AIS patients, prophylactic antiseizure medication is not recommended as it does not prevent seizures or improve functional outcome.
Prophylactic antiseizure medication is not beneficial for patients with spontaneous ICH who have no evidence of seizures with regard to functional outcomes, long-term seizure control, or mortality.

consider: After an unprovoked poststroke seizure, choose the antiseizure drug by patient factors (AHA 2026, COR 1).
Document the indication and a review date for any antiseizure drug continued at discharge.
aSAH with a seizure at onset: treat for no more than 7 days; longer courses do not reduce later seizures.

topics.summary: Do not settle prognosis on day 1. recommendations.text: A baseline severity score alone is not recommended as the sole basis for forecasting individual prognosis or deciding to limit life-sustaining treatment in patients with spontaneous ICH.

consider: Identify sedation, medical instability and other confounders before discussing prognosis.
Explain the outcome being estimated, the time horizon and the range of uncertainty.
Revisit recovery over time and incorporate what outcomes the patient would value.
topics.caution: Premature withdrawal can distort both individual care and the evidence used to estimate prognosis.

topics.title: RCVS and PRES
topics.summary: Recurrent thunderclap headaches with segmental cerebral vasoconstriction suggest RCVS; over half of cases are postpartum or follow adrenergic or serotonergic drugs. Vasoconstriction peaks 2–3 weeks after onset and resolves within 3 months, and stroke can follow initially normal imaging. RCVS2 (thunderclap headache, carotid involvement, vasoconstrictive trigger, sex, SAH; range −2 to +10): ≥5 was 99% specific and 90% sensitive for RCVS; ≤2 was 100% specific for excluding it, including against PACNS. PRES (bilateral subcortical vasogenic edema) follows BP fluctuation, renal failure, cytotoxic drugs, autoimmune disease or eclampsia, and usually resolves.
consider: Exclude aneurysmal SAH first and remove vasoactive triggers.
Repeat vessel imaging if early imaging is normal but suspicion persists.
Nimodipine may ease thunderclap headache within 48 h but has no proven effect on stroke or hemorrhage.
PRES: treat the driver (BP, drug, eclampsia) and watch for hemorrhage or posterior-fossa edema with hydrocephalus.
topics.caution: Evidence is observational; RCVS2 was derived from 30 RCVS patients at one center.

Supportive findings: adjacent arterial dissection or occlusion (20%) and vertebral body infarction (9%); CSF was inflammatory in only 8%.

Selective pain and temperature loss (39%) and a stuttering course (23%) occur; do not label transverse myelitis too early.
Apply the proposed definite, probable and possible criteria, and exclude cord compression.

topics.title: aSAH critical care and CSF diversion
topics.summary: Keep euvolemia (AHA 2023, 2a); induced hypervolemia and prophylactic hemodynamic augmentation are harmful (COR 3). Monitor for DCI with frequent exams, TCD, and CTA or CT perfusion when the exam is unreliable (2a). Symptomatic vasospasm: raising SBP, intra-arterial vasodilators or angioplasty may be reasonable (2b). Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus: EVD and/or lumbar drainage (COR 1) under a bundled EVD protocol. EARLYDRAIN (lumbar drain after securing) reduced poor outcome, but ESO 2026 makes no recommendation on prophylactic lumbar drainage.
consider: Do not drain CSF for radiological hydrocephalus alone when consciousness is normal (ESO consensus).
Liberal transfusion (Hb ≤10 g/dL) did not improve 12-month outcome (SAHaRA).
Start VTE prophylaxis once the aneurysm is secured (COR 1).
topics.caution: Drain management needs the full neurosurgical protocol.

topics.title: New and adjunct therapies: match the evidence
topics.summary: Asundexian (factor XIa inhibitor) added to antiplatelets reduced ischemic stroke after noncardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA (OCEANIC-STROKE 6.2 vs 8.4%; major bleeding 1.9 vs 1.7%) but was worse than apixaban in AF (OCEANIC-AF). Nerinetide (ESCAPE-NEXT), prehospital remote ischemic conditioning (RESIST) and colchicine (CONVINCE, CHANCE-3) were neutral; SERIC-EVT (conditioning after EVT) is a single positive trial.
consider: Compare the population, background therapy and primary endpoint with your patient before applying a new result.
Separate confirmatory results from subgroup signals, and look for independent replication.
Confirm regulatory approval and local availability before using any new agent.
topics.caution: Neuroprotective agents and IV argatroban are not recommended outside trials (AHA 2026, COR 3).

topics.title: Rapid appraisal of a trial or guideline
topics.summary: Use a structured appraisal before converting a study headline into a clinical decision: population, comparison, outcome, uncertainty and applicability.
consider: Is the outcome patient-important, and is the quoted result the prespecified primary analysis?
Compare absolute and relative effects, confidence intervals, missing data and harms.
Check whether subgroup, noninferiority or composite-endpoint claims support the proposed inference.
topics.caution: A neutral superiority trial does not prove equivalence.

topics.title: ICH expansion and intraventricular extension
topics.summary: No hemostatic drug improves function: recombinant factor VIIa within 2 h (FASTEST) slowed growth by 3.7 mL but did not change 180-day mRS (cOR 1.09) and increased life-threatening thromboembolism (RR 3.41); tranexamic acid (TICH-2) also gave no functional benefit (aOR 0.88). IVH with hydrocephalus and reduced consciousness: EVD (AHA 2022, COR 1). Intraventricular alteplase through an EVD lowered 180-day mortality (18 vs 29%) without improving mRS ≤3 and increased mRS 5 (CLEAR III).
consider: Is the problem expansion, ventricular obstruction, hydrocephalus or mass effect?
Repeat CT within 24 h, sooner with any decline, to catch expansion.
Discuss procedural risks and patient-valued outcomes with neurosurgery.
topics.caution: Lower mortality without functional gain can mean more survivors with severe disability.

topics.title: Sudden severe headache and suspected SAH
topics.summary: Sudden severe headache warrants prompt evaluation for SAH and other serious causes. Interpret a negative CT with the onset interval, neurologic findings, scanner quality and reader expertise.
consider: Establish time to peak pain, onset time, examination findings and whether the presentation fits the source population.

AHA/ASA 2023 recommends LP after a negative CT when presentation is more than 6 hours after onset or there is a new neurologic deficit; early CT-only assessment has specific quality and examination requirements.
ACEP 2019 allows LP or CTA when SAH risk remains after negative CT, with shared discussion of limitations. Review these differing recommendations with the local diagnostic pathway.
topics.caution: A negative CT is not universal clearance, and CTA can find an incidental aneurysm.

studies.title: ELAN — timing of anticoagulation after AF-associated stroke
studies.headline: Early DOAC: composite 2.9 vs 4.1% (difference not significant)
studies.question: How did earlier DOAC initiation compare with a later schedule?
studies.population: 2,013 people with acute ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation.
studies.comparison: Earlier: within 48 hours for minor/moderate stroke or days 6–7 for major stroke. Later: days 3–4, 6–7 or 12–14, respectively.
studies.result: The 30-day composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage or vascular death was 2.9% versus 4.1% (risk difference −1.18 percentage points; 95% CI −2.84 to 0.47). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.2% in both groups.
studies.limits: The confidence interval includes no difference. Trial severity categories and exclusions require review; this is not an automatic start-date rule.

studies.title: OPTIMAS — early versus delayed DOAC initiation
studies.headline: DOAC ≤4 days noninferior to days 7–14 (3.3% each)
studies.question: Was initiation within four days noninferior to starting at 7–14 days?
studies.population: 3,621 analyzed adults with AF-associated ischemic stroke at 100 UK hospitals; clinicians were uncertain about timing.
studies.comparison: DOAC initiation within four days versus days 7–14.
studies.result: At 90 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 3.3% of each group. Noninferiority met the two-percentage-point margin; superiority was not demonstrated. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.6% versus 0.7%.
studies.limits: Open-label treatment with masked adjudication. Apply the trial selection criteria; identical observed rates do not prove identical individual risk.

studies.result: Death or disability (mRS 4–6) at three months was 38.7% versus 37.7% (adjusted RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.85–1.27). Renal adverse events within seven days were more frequent with intensive treatment: 9.0% versus 4.0% (P=0.002).

studies.title: INTERACT3 — coordinated acute ICH care bundle
studies.headline: ICH care bundle: better mRS (cOR 0.86)
studies.question: Did implementing a coordinated physiological-care bundle improve function?
studies.population: 7,036 adults with spontaneous ICH within six hours at 121 hospitals in ten countries; 6,255 had primary-outcome data.
studies.comparison: Hospital implementation of early BP lowering, glucose and temperature management, and warfarin reversal for abnormal values versus usual care; stepped-wedge cluster randomization.
studies.result: At six months the bundle improved the ordinal mRS distribution (common OR for worse outcome 0.86; 95% CI 0.76–0.97). Serious adverse events occurred in 16.0% versus 20.1%.

studies.question: Did intermittent pneumatic compression reduce proximal DVT?

studies.headline: PEG vs nasogastric: more death or poor outcome (+7.8 points)
studies.question: Should PEG routinely replace nasogastric feeding early after stroke?

studies.comparison: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) versus nasogastric feeding.

studies.title: SHINE — intensive glucose control in acute ischemic stroke
studies.headline: Intensive insulin: no benefit; severe hypoglycemia 2.6%
studies.question: Did intensive insulin treatment improve 90-day function?
studies.population: 1,151 adults with hyperglycemic ischemic stroke enrolled within 12 hours at 63 US sites.
studies.comparison: IV insulin targeting glucose 80–130 mg/dL versus subcutaneous sliding-scale insulin targeting 80–179 mg/dL for up to 72 hours.

studies.title: DESTINY II — hemicraniectomy in older patients
studies.headline: Hemicraniectomy 61–82 y: survival with mRS 0–4 38 vs 18%
studies.question: What survival and disability tradeoff accompanied surgery after age 60?
studies.population: 112 patients aged 61–82 with malignant middle-cerebral-artery infarction, randomized within 48 hours; median age 70.
studies.comparison: Hemicraniectomy versus conservative intensive-care treatment.
studies.result: At six months, survival with mRS 0–4 was 38% versus 18% (OR 2.91; 95% CI 1.06–7.49). Mortality was 33% versus 70%. No participant achieved mRS 0–2; most survivors needed help with bodily needs. Infections were more frequent after surgery.

studies.title: RESTART — antiplatelet therapy after antithrombotic-associated ICH
studies.headline: Antiplatelet restart after ICH: recurrent ICH 4 vs 9% (NS)
studies.question: Did restarting antiplatelet therapy increase recurrent ICH?
studies.population: 537 ICH survivors previously taking antithrombotic therapy for occlusive vascular disease; randomized a median of 76 days after ICH.
studies.comparison: Start versus avoid antiplatelet therapy.

studies.title: EARLYDRAIN — lumbar CSF drainage after secured aSAH
studies.headline: Lumbar drain after aSAH: mRS 3–6 32.6 vs 44.8%
studies.question: Did early lumbar drainage improve outcome after aneurysm treatment?
studies.population: 287 analyzable adults with aneurysmal SAH across clinical grades; aneurysms were clipped or coiled within 48 hours.
studies.comparison: Additional lumbar drainage at 5 mL/hour, begun within 72 hours, versus standard care.
studies.result: Six-month mRS 3–6 occurred in 32.6% versus 44.8% (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.52–0.98). Secondary infarction at discharge was 28.5% versus 39.9%. Drain complications included a pressure gradient stopping drainage, local infection and a retained torn catheter.

studies.title: SAHaRA — liberal versus restrictive transfusion in aSAH
studies.headline: Liberal transfusion in aSAH: no benefit (33.5 vs 37.7%)
studies.question: Did a more liberal transfusion threshold improve neurological outcome?
studies.population: 742 critically ill adults with acute aneurysmal SAH and anemia at 23 centers; 725 contributed to the primary analysis.
studies.comparison: Mandatory red-cell transfusion at hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL versus optional transfusion at ≤8 g/dL.
studies.result: At 12 months, unfavorable outcome (mRS ≥4) occurred in 33.5% versus 37.7% (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.72–1.09; P=0.22). Functional-independence and quality-of-life measures did not show significant differences; adverse-event incidence was similar.
studies.limits: No superiority was demonstrated; the confidence interval does not establish equivalence. The restrictive strategy allowed clinical discretion and must not be recast as mandatory transfusion at 8 g/dL or a universal rule for all acute brain injuries.

studies.title: CADISS — antiplatelet versus anticoagulant treatment for dissection
studies.headline: Dissection: antiplatelet vs anticoagulant, few events (3 vs 1)
studies.question: Did antithrombotic strategy alter early stroke recurrence?
studies.population: 250 patients with symptomatic extracranial carotid or vertebral dissection within seven days; central imaging review did not confirm dissection in 52.
studies.comparison: Clinician-selected antiplatelet versus anticoagulant treatment for three months.
